OPS05-BP01 Develop and test runbooks to perform procedures
A runbook is a documented procedure that produces the same outcome
    every time, no matter who runs it. Teams use runbooks for routine
    and high-stakes work, from onboarding an engineer to deploying a
    release or recovering from an incident. Without them, operations
    depend on memory and habit, which produces inconsistent results and
    more errors.
Desired outcome:
Your team maintains a library of step-by-step runbooks, each
        stating a desired outcome, the required tools and permissions,
        and the error-handling and escalation path.
Your runbooks live in a central, version-controlled location
        that all team members can find and use.
Your runbook content stays current because updates follow your
        change management process as procedures evolve.
You automate your frequently used runbooks, so routine work runs
        consistently with little manual effort.
Common anti-patterns:
Team members rely on memory to complete each step of a recurring
        process.
Engineers deploy changes manually without a checklist or
        documented procedure.
Two people perform the same task and produce different results
        because the steps are undocumented.
Runbooks drift out of sync with the systems and automation they
        describe.
Benefits of establishing this best
    practice:
Manual tasks produce fewer errors because every step is written
        down and validated.
Operations run consistently no matter who performs them.
New team members become productive sooner by following
        documented procedures.
Automating runbooks reduces repetitive manual work and frees
        engineers for higher-value tasks.
Level of risk exposed if this best practice
    is not established:
Medium
Implementation guidance
When you create a runbook, state the desired outcome first, then
      list the tools, permissions, and steps needed to reach it. Name an
      owner so responsibility for keeping the runbook current is clear.
Start with text runbooks and plan to automate. Every manual run is
      a chance for a skipped or misread step, so automating short,
      frequently used procedures first returns the investment quickly
      and builds the skill to automate harder cases. Keep judgment
      calls, rare procedures, and steps that need human approval manual
      while you automate the repetitive core.
Drift is common, as the system and automation might change while
      the runbook does not and someone follows the stale version during
      an incident. Tie runbook updates to your change management process
      to keep them current. Include error handling for when a step fails
      and an escalation path for when the procedure cannot resolve the
      problem.
Runbooks and playbooks pair together but solve different problems.
      A runbook executes a known procedure to reach a known outcome. A
      playbook guides investigation when the outcome is not yet known,
      such as diagnosing why a deployment failed. When a playbook
      identifies a root cause, it points to the runbook that resolves
      it. Keep the two separate so a runbook does not become an
      open-ended troubleshooting guide.
On AWS, use
AWS Systems Manager Automation
to turn documented procedures
      into automation runbooks that run against your workload, on demand
      or in response to events. Use the low-code
visual design experience
to build them. For common operational
      issues, Support maintains
Support self-service runbooks
that troubleshoot resources,
      monitor for network issues, and collect logs.
Implementation steps
Choose a central
            repository:
Use your existing documentation wiki
            or version control system as the home for your runbook
            library. Version control gives you history, review, and
            rollback for procedures, and a single known location stops
            copies from drifting apart. Create a new repository only if
            no suitable store exists.
Select a procedure to document
            first:
Pick a process that runs semi-regularly,
            has a small number of steps, and fails with low impact.
            Starting small builds the habit and the template before you
            tackle recovery or deployment procedures where mistakes are
            costly.
Draft the runbook from a standard
            template:
Create a document from a shared
            template so every runbook records the same structure and
            metadata. Fill in the title, the runbook info, and each step
            in order. Keeping the runbook in Markdown makes it portable
            across most automation systems.
# Runbook title
## Runbook info
| Runbook ID | Description | Tools used | Special permissions | Author | Last updated | Escalation contact |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| RUN001 | What is this runbook for and what outcome does it produce? | Tools | Permissions | Your name | 2026-01-01 | Escalation name |
## Steps

2. Step two
Validate the runbook with a
            peer:
Give the draft to a team member who did not
            write it and have them perform the procedure using only the
            written steps. Update anything that is missing, ambiguous,
            or out of order. This confirms the runbook works without the
            author present.
Publish and announce the
            runbook:
Publish the validated runbook to your
            central store and tell your team and stakeholders where to
            find it. Record the owner so responsibility for keeping it
            current is clear.
Automate mature runbooks:
As your library grows, convert stable, frequently used text
            runbooks into automation with
AWS Systems Manager Automation
. The low-code
visual design experience
helps you build automation
            runbooks, and you can run them in response to events to
            reduce manual effort. Keep the automated version and its
            documentation in sync.
Kiro
can be used
            accelerate the development of runbooks and help to keep the
            documentation consistent.
